lesson.title: Asking Python to Compare Two Values
lesson.summary: Comparison operators such as ==, !=, <, >, <=, and >= take two values and produce a boolean result, making them the most common way to build a boolean expression.
lesson.body:
A comparison operator takes two values, one on each side, and asks a specific question about how they relate: are they equal, is the left one smaller, is the right one at least as large. Python answers that question by producing a boolean expression, one that evaluates to True or False exactly as described in the previous section. There are six comparison operators in Python: == for equal, != for not equal, < for less than, > for greater than, <= for less than or equal to, and >= for greater than or equal to. Each one is a complete expression once it has two operands, and the value it produces is always a bool, never anything else.

These operators are not limited to numbers. Python defines meaningful comparisons for strings, comparing them character by character using their underlying character codes, and for many other types as well. What every comparison operator has in common is that it never modifies either operand; it only inspects them and reports a result. That single restriction is what makes comparisons safe to use anywhere an expression is expected, including inside more complicated boolean expressions built with and, or, and not.

Trace this example carefully:

x = 7
y = 10
result = (x + 3) == y
print(result)

Python evaluates the arithmetic first, because the parentheses and normal precedence rules require x + 3 to become a single value before the comparison can happen. x + 3 evaluates to 10. Now the comparison is effectively 10 == y, and since y is 10, both sides hold the same value, so the expression evaluates to True. That boolean value, not the number 10, is what gets assigned to result.

A common early mistake is confusing = with ==. A single equals sign is the assignment operator; it stores a value in a variable and does not produce a comparison. A double equals sign is the comparison operator; it never changes a variable, it only checks whether two values match and hands back True or False. Python actually raises a SyntaxError if you try to use = where an expression like a condition is required, which catches many of these mistakes early, but the conceptual difference between assigning and asking is worth keeping straight regardless. The next two sections look closely at two natural groupings of these operators: equality, using == and !=, and ordering, using <, >, <=, and >=.

Not every pair of types can be compared with every operator. Python allows == and != between values of any type and simply returns False if the two values are too different to ever be equal, so 5 == "5" evaluates to False rather than raising an error. Ordering operators are stricter: writing 5 < "5" raises a TypeError, because Python has no defined notion of whether a number comes before a string. This asymmetry is worth remembering when combining values pulled from different sources, such as user input, which always arrives as a string, and a stored number; comparing them directly with < or > will crash the program unless one side is first converted to match the other's type.
